lesson.title: What a Circuit Does on Its Own
lesson.summary: The natural response is the part of a circuit's behavior that comes purely from energy already stored in its capacitor or inductor, independent of any source, and separating it from the forced response explains why total behavior is the sum of two simpler pieces.
lesson.body:
Every first-order transient studied so far can be split into two separate causes acting together: the fact that a source is driving the circuit, and the fact that the capacitor or inductor already had some energy stored in it before the clock started. The piece of the response that comes purely from that stored energy, with the source imagined turned off, is called the natural response. The piece that comes purely from the source, with the initial condition imagined to be zero, is called the forced response. Because RC and RL circuits are linear, the actual measured response is simply the sum of these two pieces, a direct application of superposition.

Some of the transients already covered were secretly pure natural response. RC discharging and RL de-energizing both started with stored energy, V0 on a capacitor or I0 in an inductor, and no source left in the loop at all, so their entire exponential decay was the natural response by itself, x_n(t) = x(0)*e^(-t/tau). RC charging and RL energizing, on the other hand, started from zero initial energy, so what was computed there was actually the forced response alone, the circuit's answer to the source with no history to add in. The general exponential formula from before is really always computing natural plus forced, it is just that in those earlier examples one of the two pieces happened to be zero.

The natural response always has the same shape regardless of what is driving the rest of the circuit: it starts at whatever the initial condition contributed and decays toward zero with the circuit's own time constant, x_n(t) = x_n(0)*e^(-t/tau). It decays to zero, not to some other value, because natural response literally means the source is switched off, so there is nothing for the circuit to settle toward except zero. This is the part of the response that reflects the circuit's memory of its past.

Here is a case where both pieces are doing real work at once. Suppose a capacitor already sitting at V0 = 5 V, an initial condition left over from an earlier part of the circuit's history, is switched into a new loop with a fresh source Vs = 20 V, R = 2 k ohms, and C = 50 microfarads. The time constant is tau = RC = 2000*0.00005 = 0.1 seconds. The forced response, what this circuit would do if it had started at zero, is v_f(t) = 20*(1 - e^(-t/0.1)). The natural response, what the 5 V initial condition alone would produce with the source turned off, is v_n(t) = 5*e^(-t/0.1). At t = 100 ms, one time constant, v_f = 20*(1 - 0.3679) = 20*0.6321 = 12.64 V and v_n = 5*0.3679 = 1.84 V. Adding them, v(t) = 12.64 + 1.84 = 14.48 V, which matches applying the general exponential formula directly with x_initial = 5 and x_final = 20: 20 + (5 - 20)*e^-1 = 20 - 15*0.3679 = 20 - 5.52 = 14.48 V.

Splitting the response this way is more than bookkeeping. It shows exactly which part of a circuit's behavior depends on its past, the natural response built from initial conditions, and which part depends only on what is happening right now, the forced response built from the source. Any first-order circuit's full story is these two independent stories, added together.
